ddx.step1_summary:
- Chief complaint: Left-sided hearing loss and left facial numbness
- Symptom details: ~3 weeks of decreased hearing in the left ear; constant numbness around the left ear and along the left jawline; intermittent left-sided tinnitus; occasional dizziness associated with the ringing. Denies ear pain, ear discharge, ear itch, fever, dysphagia, dysarthria, limb weakness/numbness, or visual changes.
- Past medical history: Nasal polyps; remote history of labyrinthitis; possible dyspepsia (uses Rennies PRN). No other chronic illnesses reported.
- Medications/allergies: PRN intranasal spray for nasal polyps (name unknown); PRN antacid (Rennies). Allergy: latex.
- Family/social history: Brother with neurofibromatosis (type unspecified). Works as a jockey; lives with partner; no pets. No noise exposure or trauma reported in this visit.
- Vitals/exam: Not available (telemedicine; no focal exam performed).
- Labs/imaging: None mentioned.

V: AICA/internal auditory artery ischemia or brainstem (pontine) stroke: Can cause acute unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, vertigo, and ipsilateral facial sensory symptoms; less likely given subacute 3-week course without other focal deficits.
Vascular loop compression of CN VIII: Rare cause of tinnitus and hearing symptoms; does not readily explain facial numbness.
I: Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus): Can cause hearing loss, tinnitus/vertigo with facial nerve involvement; typically painful with vesicular rash and facial weakness, which are absent here.
Viral labyrinthitis/vestibular neuritis: Can cause acute hearing loss with vertigo/tinnitus, often post-viral; facial numbness is atypical.
Lyme disease (neuroborreliosis): Can produce cranial neuropathies and audiovestibular symptoms; exposure history not provided.
N: Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma): Classic for unilateral SNHL, tinnitus, imbalance; larger lesions can cause facial or trigeminal sensory changes. Family history of neurofibromatosis raises suspicion.
Cerebellopontine angle meningioma: Can mimic vestibular schwannoma with unilateral hearing loss and cranial nerve symptoms.
D: Otosclerosis: Progressive conductive hearing loss; typically no facial numbness and often bilateral; less consistent with this case.
Presbycusis: Age-related bilateral SNHL; not consistent with unilateral symptoms at age 40.
Vitamin B12 deficiency: Can cause neuropathy; unilateral focal cranial neuropathy with hearing loss is unlikely.
I2: Ototoxicity (e.g., aminoglycosides, loop diuretics): Can cause bilateral SNHL/tinnitus; patient not on such agents.
Noise-induced hearing loss: Typically bilateral high-frequency loss; no clear exposure history.
C: Neurofibromatosis type 2: Predisposes to bilateral vestibular schwannomas and other cranial nerve tumors; a unilateral presentation can occur early. Brother with neurofibromatosis increases concern for a related tumor syndrome.
A: Autoimmune inner ear disease: Fluctuating hearing loss (often bilateral) +/- tinnitus/vertigo; facial numbness is not typical.
Sarcoidosis (neurosarcoid): Can cause cranial neuropathies and audiovestibular symptoms; no systemic features reported.
T: Temporal bone/inner ear trauma: Could cause unilateral hearing loss and vestibular symptoms; no trauma reported.
TMJ dysfunction: Can cause peri-auricular symptoms; does not explain sensorineural hearing loss or persistent facial numbness.
E: Diabetes mellitus: Can cause cranial neuropathies and vestibular dysfunction; unilateral hearing loss with isolated facial numbness is atypical.
Hypothyroidism: Can contribute to hearing loss; would not explain focal facial numbness.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma), consider NF2-related vs sporadic
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Best unifying diagnosis for unilateral progressive hearing loss, tinnitus, intermittent imbalance, and ipsilateral facial numbness; family history of neurofibromatosis increases pre-test probability.
supporting_evidence: Intermittent left-sided tinnitus and occasional dizziness
Persistent ipsilateral facial numbness around the ear and jawline (possible trigeminal/facial nerve involvement)
Brother with neurofibromatosis (tumor predisposition, especially NF2 for vestibular schwannomas)
opposing_evidence: Time course of only a few weeks is shorter than the typical months to years progression
No objective exam findings documented yet
Age 40 is slightly younger than average sporadic cases but compatible, particularly if familial predisposition

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Can present with unilateral hearing change, tinnitus, and episodic vertigo; does not typically cause facial numbness.
opposing_evidence: Hearing loss described as persistent rather than fluctuating in discrete attacks

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Can cause audiovestibular symptoms and facial nerve involvement, but classic features (ear pain, vesicular rash, facial weakness) are absent.
supporting_evidence: Hearing loss with tinnitus and dizziness can occur
Facial nerve territory symptoms near the ear
opposing_evidence: No facial weakness (patient reports numbness, not paresis)

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Multiple sclerosis (brainstem demyelination affecting CN V/VIII pathways)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Could explain facial sensory symptoms and audiovestibular complaints in a 40-year-old woman, though less typical without other neurologic signs or prior episodes.
supporting_evidence: Facial numbness consistent with trigeminal pathway involvement
Audiovestibular symptoms could occur with brainstem lesions
opposing_evidence: No other neurologic deficits or history of relapsing symptoms
Hearing loss is a less common presentation

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Idiopathic sudden sensorineural hearing loss / viral labyrinthitis
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Subacute hearing loss with tinnitus/dizziness fits, but facial numbness and absence of viral prodrome or otologic pain make it less likely.
supporting_evidence: Hearing loss with intermittent tinnitus and occasional dizziness
opposing_evidence: No preceding viral symptoms, ear pain, or acute onset described
